articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities for Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Activities, Imposes New Cuba Sanctions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting entities involved in cyber-related malicious activities and transnational criminal organizations.
Concurrently, OFAC also imposed new sanctions related to Cuba and published a Cuba-related determination, further restricting transactions with the island nation.
These actions underscore the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to combat cybercrime, disrupt illicit financial networks, and maintain pressure on the Cuban regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran Sanctions, Updates Listings, Issues Alert on Shadow Fleet, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and updates to existing Iran-related listings on November 4, 2026.

In conjunction with these actions, OFAC published an alert titled 'Iranian Shadow Fleet Reliance on False Flags for Sanctions Evasion,' highlighting the risks associated with providing services to vessels using deceptive practices to circumvent U.S. sanctions on Iran.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License 5AA, 'Authorizing Certain Transactions Related to the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 Percent Bond on or After December 18, 2026,' and an amended Frequently Asked Question (FAQ 595).

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026.
This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran, reflecting ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions program.
Specific details of the amendments are available on OFAC's recent actions page, providing guidance for compliance with the updated regulations.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo Sanctions Programs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities under both the North Korea sanctions program and the Democratic Republic of the Congo-related sanctions program.
These actions aim to counter threats posed by North Korea's weapons of mass destruction programs and address human rights abuses and corruption in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to using sanctions to promote international security and human rights.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based artificial intelligence and cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme exported networking equipment and related services from the United States to a Russian missile and air defense manufacturer that was majority-owned by a designated Russian state-owned company.

OFAC determined that Extreme acted with reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions by failing to conduct sufficient due diligence and ignoring warning signs that the Russian defense manufacturer was the ultimate recipient of the goods, despite the violations being voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) amended several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, as part of its ongoing review of published guidance.
The updated FAQs, including numbers 10, 32-36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53, address topics such as blocking and rejecting transactions, and filing reports with OFAC.
These revisions aim to ensure that information remains current and provide clarity for financial institutions and other entities on compliance procedures for U.S. sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran Sanctions, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, and Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026.
Concurrently, OFAC removed certain individuals and entities from its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List under the Belarus and North Korea sanctions programs.
Additionally, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended several Frequently Asked Questions, providing updated guidance for various transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued PAIPA General License 1, 'Transactions Authorized Pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations,' and PAIPA General License 2, 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving Certain Entities Blocked on October 19, 2026.'

These actions aim to protect American intellectual property by targeting entities involved in theft and illicit activities, while also providing guidance for authorized transactions and wind-down periods.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-related General License for Earthquake Relief
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Venezuela-related General License 60A, 'Authorizing Transactions Related to Earthquake Relief Efforts in Venezuela,' on October 16, 2026.
This amended general license aims to facilitate humanitarian aid and relief efforts following recent earthquake activity in Venezuela.
OFAC also issued one amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 1263, to provide further clarification on the scope of authorized transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran and Cuba Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026.
In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions.
These actions reflect the U.S. government's continued use of sanctions to address perceived threats from Iran and Cuba.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

The violations involved the export of networking equipment and services to a Russian missile and air defense manufacturer that was a blocked person due to its majority ownership by a designated Russian state-owned company.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, emphasizing the importance of thorough sanctions-related diligence, especially when acquiring companies or assets, and maintaining oversight of foreign operations.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 in Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs.

These violations occurred when the bank processed correspondent banking payments through blocked banks, allowed designated individuals to make payments and withdraw funds due to poor sanctions alert calibration, failed to promptly update watchlists, and mishandled business accounts associated with blocked persons.

The settlement reflects OFAC's determination that the apparent violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, with no reduction to the base penalty for remedial measures or cooperation.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.
The specific details of the violations were not immediately available but typically involve breaches of sanctions programs related to prohibited transactions or dealings with sanctioned entities.
This enforcement action underscores OFAC's continued focus on ensuring compliance across various industries, including logistics and shipping.

articles.headline: Individual Pays $1,427,230 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle their potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

While the specific details of the individual's violations were not publicly detailed in the immediate announcement, such penalties often arise from unauthorized transactions with sanctioned countries or entities.
This settlement highlights OFAC's enforcement efforts against individuals who engage in activities that contravene U.S. sanctions policy.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $60,764
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

The nature of the violations was not immediately specified, but OFAC enforcement actions against companies typically involve issues such as exporting goods to sanctioned destinations or engaging in transactions with sanctioned parties.
This settlement serves as a reminder for companies to maintain robust compliance programs to avoid inadvertent breaches of U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Pays $1,050,000 for Indirect Dealings with Sanctioned Russian Bank
body: FTI Consulting, Inc., a Washington D.C.-based international consulting firm, has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle its potential civil liability for six apparent violations of OFAC sanctions targeting Russia's financial sector.

Between April 2019 and May 2021, FTI indirectly dealt in prohibited debt of VTB Bank OAO, a Russian state-owned bank on OFAC's Sectoral Sanctions Identification List, by extending debt beyond the permissible 14-day tenor through unpaid invoices.

OFAC determined that FTI recklessly missed multiple warning signs, despite the violations being non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, underscoring the importance of looking beyond formal arrangements to the underlying economic realities of transactions.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Settles with OFAC for $275 Million Over Iranian LPG Shipments
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), an India-based multinational, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran.

From November 2023 to June 2025, AEL purchased 32 shipments of Iranian-origin liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) disguised as Omani and Iraqi product, causing U.S. financial institutions to process approximately $192 million in U.S. dollar-denominated payments.

OFAC determined that AEL's apparent violations were egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, citing reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions despite multiple red flags and substantial harm to U.S. foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Pays $1,110,661 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

The specific details of the violations were not immediately available but typically involve failures in sanctions screening, processing prohibited transactions, or dealing with sanctioned individuals or entities.
This settlement highlights the importance for financial institutions to implement and maintain robust sanctions compliance programs to prevent such breaches.

articles.headline: Individual Pays $3,777,000 to Settle Syrian Sanctions Violations
body: A U.S. citizen residing abroad has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle potential civil liability for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations.
Between 2018 and 2021, the individual engaged in transactions that contravened U.S. sanctions against Syria, which broadly prohibit most transactions involving Syria by U.S. persons.
This significant penalty underscores OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions against individuals, even those residing outside the United States, for violations of U.S. foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Pays $1,720,000 for Violations of Counternarcotics Sanctions
body: IMG Academy, a school and athletic training facility in Florida, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle its potential civil liability for 89 apparent violations of OFAC counternarcotics sanctions.

Over five consecutive years, IMG Academy repeatedly transacted with two individuals sanctioned under the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act due to their ties to a Mexican-based drug cartel, by entering into tuition enrollment agreements and processing payments for their children.

OFAC determined that IMG Academy demonstrated reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions requirements by failing to conduct sanctions screening checks on its counterparties, despite the violations being non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.
